# Brief: decide whether we advertise in Torque again next year

The full-page advert in Torque comes up for renewal next month at a nine per
cent increase. We have run it for four years and I cannot tell you what it has
brought in. Before we sign again I want an honest answer, and if the honest
answer is that we do not know, I want to know what it would take to find out.

## Background

The advert began as a favour to a customer who edits the magazine, and it stayed
because it looks good in reception and because cancelling it would have been a
conversation. It is a full page, right-hand side, in a monthly with a claimed
circulation of thirty-one thousand and a readership the publisher puts at three
times that. Neither figure has been audited in the four years we have been
buying.

Our enquiry form has a "how did you hear about us" field. Ninety per cent of
respondents choose "other" or leave it blank, so what we have is not evidence,
and the sales team's impression — that the trade shows do the work and the
magazine does not — is also not evidence, though it is worth something.

## Questions to answer

- What the advert costs us all in, including the design time we spend each year
  refreshing it and the reprint we paid for when the new logo landed.
- Whether a tracked route is possible. A dedicated phone number or a short URL
  for the print advert would settle in six months what four years of impressions
  have not.
- What the publisher will actually commit to on circulation. If the figure is
  unaudited, the price is being set against a number nobody stands behind, and
  that is worth raising before we negotiate the increase.
- What the alternatives are for the same money. Two trade shows, a year of the
  smaller trade weekly, or the same page in the same magazine at a quarter of
  the frequency.

## Constraints

The relationship with the editor is real and worth something to us
independently of the advertising. Whatever we decide, we should decide it
deliberately and tell them early — cancelling by silence in December is how you
lose a customer as well as a magazine.

## What I want back

A page: what it costs, what we can and cannot attribute to it, one tracked route
we could put in place for next year, and a recommendation. If the recommendation
is to keep it as a relationship expense and stop calling it marketing, that is a
perfectly good answer, as long as it is written down and the budget line is
moved to match.
